prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Producer Price Index (PPI)
Description: The Producer Price Index (PPI) program measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output. The prices included in the PPI are from the first commercial transaction for many products and some services.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Handbook of Methods Producer Price Indexes Overview

Producer Price Indexes: Overview

The Producer Price Index (PPI) measures average changes in prices received by domestic producers for their output. Most of the information used in calculating producer price indexes is obtained through the systematic sampling of industries. In the mining and manufacturing sectors, price information from virtually every industry is captured. By contrast, although PPI coverage of the service sector of the economy is substantial at roughly 70 percent of total sector revenue, it is incomplete. The PPI program also includes data that track other sectors of the economy: agriculture, fishing, forestry, utilities (natural gas and electricity), and construction.

As of January 2024, the PPI program included the following indexes:

  • Price indexes for approximately 500 mining, forestry, utility, construction, manufacturing, and services industries; indexes for over 500 groupings of industries; and nearly 3,700 indexes for specific within-industry product and service categories.
  • More than 3,700 commodity price indexes for goods and about 900 for services (seasonally adjusted and not seasonally adjusted), organized by product, service, and end use.
  • Over 600 indexes for aggregate measures of price change, including the aggregation system for final demand–intermediate demand (FD–ID).

Together, these elements constitute a system of price measures designed to meet the need for both aggregate information and detailed applications, such as following price trends for specific industries and products, as well as the need for tracking price movements at a more aggregated level relative to the overall economy.

Quick Facts: Producer Price Indexes
Subject areas Prices
Key measures
  • Price change
How the data are obtained Survey of businesses
Classification Commodity, Industry
Classification system

North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)
Periodicity of data availability Monthly
Geographic detail National
Scope Private sector
Revision Information

PPI index revisions include iterative updates for the 3 interim months after first issuance prior to posting of final indexes 4 months after original publication.
Key products
  • Producer Price I

Handbook of Methods Producer Price Indexes Data sources

Producer Price Indexes: Data sources

The Producer Price Index (PPI) is a voluntary survey, and although some companies decline to participate during survey initiation and others may drop out of the program over the course of the timeframe of the sample, respondent cooperation is paramount to the success of the survey and remains steady. The PPI sampling process is divided into two stages. During the first stage, samples of producing establishments within an industry are selected from the universe of establishments for the industry. The sampled establishments are then contacted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) representatives, who attempt to solicit voluntary cooperation. If a sampled establishment agrees to provide information for the PPI survey, a second stage of sampling follows. During this second stage, the BLS representative obtains detailed product and transaction information for sampled items, including prices, describing a group of transactions that represent the full production of the firm. For a more detailed description of the PPI sampling process, see the design section of this PPI handbook.

Following initiation into the PPI survey, reporting establishments that agree to supply prices during the initiation process provide updated pricing information on an agreed-upon schedule, usually monthly, but sometimes less often. The PPI program obtains price updates through the BLS secure Internet Data Collection Facility (IDCF), permitting respondents to provide updates via the internet. Additional information for PPI survey respondents is available at the PPI respondents webpage.

All reported prices are analyzed using PPI computer systems, and price changes determined to be unusually large are flagged for further review by PPI analysts who verify the information before it is used in the calculation of indexes. These verifications include ensuring there were no material changes to product specifications, terms of transactions, or product substitutions. If any of these changes occurred, the reported price will be subject to a quality adjustment, which ensures comparability between the current and previous prices reported for the products. For a more detailed description of this process, see the calculation section.

PPI sampling frame

The universe for the PPI survey consists of roughly 5.0 million establishments comprising the covered portions of the mining, manufacturing, forestry, utility, services, and construction sectors. The PPI program constructs this list using Unemployment Insurance (UI) files taken from various state agencies. Supporting information and alternative frames may be obtained from other sources if the PPI deems these sources to be more accurate. The PPI program updates its samples on a regular basis to better represent current industry production. Over time, industries commonly experience changes in the universe of producers, as new establishments open and others close. Additionally, the various products produced by an industry change over time. Lastly, updating the sample of producers is vital to the maintenance of the PPI survey because over time some businesses that initially agree to cooperate withdraw from the survey.

8:30 a.m. (ET) Thursday, September 10, 2026

Technical information:      (202) 691-7705  *  ppi-info@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/ppi
Media contact:              (202) 691-5902  *  PressOffice@bls.gov   

                               PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - AUGUST 2026


The Producer Price Index for final demand moved up 0.4 percent in August, seasonally adjusted, 
the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices rose 0.1 percent in July 
and decreased 0.1 percent in June. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 5.4 percent for the 12 months ended in August.

In August, the index for final demand goods advanced 1.1 percent, and prices for final demand 
services increased 0.1 percent.

The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.3 percent in August after 
moving up 0.4 percent in July. For the 12 months ended in August, prices for final demand less 
foods, energy, and trade services advanced 4.7 percent.

Final Demand

Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods advanced 1.1 percent in August following 
two consecutive decreases. Over three-fourths of the broad-based rise can be attributed to prices for 
final demand energy, which moved up 4.2 percent. The indexes for final demand goods less foods 
and energy and for final demand foods increased 0.4 percent and 0.1 percent, respectively.

Product detail: Over a third of the August increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced 
to prices for diesel fuel, which jumped 24.1 percent. The indexes for gasoline, jet fuel, home heating 
oil, candy and nuts, and tobacco products also advanced. In contrast, prices for residential electric 
power fell 0.5 percent. The indexes for fresh sausage and for aluminum mill shapes also decreased. 
(See table 2.)

Final demand services: The index for final demand services edged up 0.1 percent in August, the 
third consecutive increase. The August advance can be attributed to a 2.3-percent rise in prices for 
final demand transportation and warehousing services. Conversely, the index for final demand trade 
services moved down 0.2 percent, while prices for final demand services less trade, transportation, 
and warehousing were unchanged.

Product detail: Leading the August increase in the index for final demand services, prices for truck 
transportation of freight advanced 2.0 percent. The indexes for airline passenger services, legal 
services, hospital inpatient care, and automobiles retailing (partial) also rose. In contrast, margins for 
fuels and lubricants retailing decreased 11.3 percent. The indexes for health, beauty, and optical 
goods retailing; machinery and equipment wholesaling; and portfolio management also moved lower.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Producer Price Index (PPI)
Description: The Producer Price Index (PPI) program measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output. The prices included in the PPI are from the first commercial transaction for many products and some services.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Producer Price Index (PPI): Research Report

*Current as of early October 2026. The most recent release found is August 2026 data, published September 10, 2026.*

---

## 1. Checking your description

**Your description is accurate.** It closely matches BLS's own wording. A few refinements:

- **It is a family of indexes, not one number.** BLS calls the program "Producer Price Indexes." As of January 2024 it included:
  - about 500 industry indexes, more than 500 indexes for groups of industries, and nearly 3,700 product indexes within industries
  - more than 3,700 commodity indexes for goods and about 900 for services
  - more than 600 aggregate indexes, including the Final Demand–Intermediate Demand (FD‑ID) system

  These counts were cut in 2025 (see §6).
- **"The PPI" in the news usually means the PPI for Final Demand.** This has been the headline measure since January 2014.
- **Prices are measured from the seller's side.** Sales and excise taxes are excluded. This is one key difference from the CPI, which measures what consumers pay.
- **Coverage is broad but incomplete.** Mining and manufacturing are almost fully covered. Services coverage is about 70% of sector revenue. Agriculture, fishing, forestry, utilities and construction are also tracked. Imports are not covered; BLS measures them separately in its Import/Export Price Indexes.

---

## 2. Publisher and governance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Publisher | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), U.S. Department of Labor |
| Office | Office of Prices and Living Conditions, PPI program |
| Contact | ppi-info@bls.gov · (202) 691‑7705 |
| Commissioner | Dr. Brett Matsumoto, 17th Commissioner. Nominated May 11, 2026; confirmed 51–47 on August 7, 2026; took office August 11, 2026. |

**Leadership background:** President Trump fired Commissioner Erika McEntarfer on August 1, 2025, after a weak jobs report, alleging without evidence that the numbers were rigged. William Wiatrowski served as acting commissioner in between. Matsumoto spent his career at BLS and was a senior economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers.

---

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Founding law:** 29 U.S.C. §1 (the BLS Organic Act, 1884/1888) and **29 U.S.C. §2** (collecting, collating and reporting labor statistics). The PPI survey's paperwork filing cites 29 U.S.C. §2 as its authorizing law.
- **Survey approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act:**
  - OMB control number **1220‑0008**, "Producer Price Index Survey."
  - The January 2024 renewal estimated 5,412 respondents, 665,182 responses a year, and 63,740 burden hours.
  - An earlier filing estimated the annual cost to the government at about $47 million.
  - Forms include BLS 1810A/C/C1/E (used to enroll new respondents), plus web-based monthly price updates.
- **Participation is voluntary.** Businesses are not required to respond.
- **Confidentiality:** Data are protected by the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA), which was reauthorized by the Evidence Act of 2018. Only sworn BLS employees may see individual company reports, and BLS publishes indexes, never actual prices.
- **Release rules:** The PPI is a Principal Federal Economic Indicator. Its release follows OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3 (pre-announced schedule, 8:30 a.m. ET, lock-up rules) and Directive No. 4. The OMB "Trust Regulation" (5 CFR Part 1321, 2024) sets out the agency's responsibilities to stay independent and objective.

---

## 4. History

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1902 | BLS publishes *Course of Wholesale Prices*, covering 250 items, with data back to 1890 |
| 1913 | All Commodities index launched under the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) |
| 1914 | Systematic weighting begins, based on the 1909 Census of Manufactures |
| 1922 | Indexes for beer, whiskey and liquors dropped because of Prohibition; restored in 1934 |
| 1930 | Monthly *Wholesale Prices and Indexes* begins |
| 1937 | Switch from a chain-type formula to a fixed-base formula |
| 1947 | More than 1,800 indexes |
| 1952 | "Stage of processing" aggregation introduced |
| 1967 | Industry indexes based on the SIC classification introduced |
| 1976–78 | WPI renamed PPI. Finished Goods becomes the headline. Probability sampling begins. *(BLS's Handbook timeline says 1976; many older BLS sources say 1978. Cite carefully.)* |
| 1985 | First services indexes (line-haul railroads) |
| 1986 | Hedonic quality adjustment; regular resampling of industries begins |
| 1988 | Rebased to 1982 = 100 (still the commodity index base) |
| 2004 | Industry indexes move from SIC to NAICS |
| 2009 | Services and construction added to the commodity system |
| 2011 | Online data collection |
| **2014** | **FD‑ID system replaces Finished Goods as the headline** |
| 2023 | Weights updated to 2017 values of shipments; commodity indexes mapped to the North American Product Classification System (NAPCS) |
| 2025 | About 350 indexes cut; collection reduced for resource reasons |
| 2026 | FD‑ID allocations updated to the 2017 Input‑Output tables; release tables revised (Feb. 27, 2026) |

---

## 5. Methods (for data scientists)

- **Sampling frame:** about 5.0 million establishments, drawn from state Unemployment Insurance files.
- **Two-stage sampling:** establishments are selected with probability proportional to size, then specific items and transaction terms within each establishment.
- **Volume:** more than 44,000 price quotes per month, according to the 2026 technical note.
- **Pricing date:** the Tuesday of the week containing the 13th of the month. BLS asks for actual transaction prices rather than list prices.
- **Formula:** a modified Laspeyres index. Weights come from Economic Census values of shipments (currently 2017).
- **Quality adjustment:** prices are adjusted when product specifications change, including hedonic methods for some products.
- **Three structures:**
  1. FD‑ID, organized by type of buyer and stage of production
  2. Commodity, organized by product or end use
  3. Industry net output, by NAICS
- **Base periods:** commodity indexes use 1982 = 100. Industry indexes are based to the month they were introduced.
- **Revisions:**
  - Unadjusted indexes are final four months after first publication.
  - Seasonal factors are recalculated each January, which revises seasonally adjusted data for the past five years.
  - Since 2021, interim values are published to three decimal places.
- **Resampling:** industries are resampled on a regular cycle (for example, 22 industries in June 2026). Detailed indexes may be added, dropped or recoded, so long-run series can break.
- **Suppression:** detailed indexes can be withheld temporarily if too few companies respond. BLS advises switching to a broader group index or a similar commodity index.

**Useful series IDs:**
- Final Demand: WPUFD4 (unadjusted) / WPSFD4 (seasonally adjusted)
- Core measures: WPSFD49104 (less foods and energy) and WPSFD49116 (less foods, energy and trade)
- Industry series start with "PCU"; commodity series start with "WPU"/"WPS"
- FRED mirrors include PPIFIS (Final Demand) and PPIACO (All Commodities, back to 1913)

---

## 6. Recent disruptions (2025–2026)

1. **About 350 indexes eliminated** (announced June 18, 2025). Cuts reached FD‑ID, special, industry and commodity indexes:
   - FD‑ID cuts took effect with July 2025 data (released Aug. 14, 2025). They included final demand less foods and energy variants and selected textile indexes.
   - Industry cuts took effect with October 2025 data; commodity cuts with January 2026 data.
   - The entire commodity group 04 (hides, skins and leather) was dropped. LIFOPro reports this affects LIFO inventory accounting.
   - BLS said discontinued series would be moved to archive databases only "as resources allow."
2. **Government shutdown, fall 2025:**
   - September 2025 PPI was delayed from Oct. 16 to Nov. 25, 2025.
   - **No October 2025 news release was issued.** October data came out with the November release on Jan. 14, 2026.
   - The October 2025 Detailed Report is listed as "Not Available."
3. **Oversight and budget:**
   - In September 2025 the Labor Department's Inspector General began reviewing BLS data-collection problems, citing the reduced CPI and PPI collection.
   - A separate Inspector General audit (June 26, 2026) covered early or improper data releases in 2024. Those incidents involved CPI and jobs data, not PPI.
   - The FY2026 budget request proposed cutting BLS funding for inflation data by about 8%.

---

## 7. Users and uses

- **Monetary policy and forecasting:** The Federal Reserve and private forecasters treat PPI as an early signal of inflation, and its components feed estimates of the PCE price index.
- **National accounts:** BEA uses PPIs to remove inflation from GDP, industry output and PCE figures. BLS uses them in its productivity statistics.
- **Contract escalation:** Long-term contracts and purchase agreements use PPIs to adjust prices automatically, including federal contracts under the FAR economic price adjustment clauses. BLS runs a dedicated contract escalation guide.
- **Tax and accounting:** The IRS Inventory Price Index Computation (IPIC) method for LIFO inventory accounting relies on PPI (Treas. Reg. §1.472‑8).
- **Health and federal payment policy:** CMS input-price "market baskets" use PPIs for many cost categories.
- **Business:** pricing, purchasing, budgeting, inventory valuation, and comparing a firm's prices to its industry.
- **Finance:** PPI is a market-moving release. Traders, analysts and journalists watch it closely.
- **Researchers:** pass-through of costs to consumer prices, supply-chain shocks, tariffs, industrial organization.

---

## 8. Public benefits

- It is a free, consistent, nationally representative measure of business-to-business prices, covering about 130 years.
- It provides an early warning of consumer inflation, which supports interest-rate decisions and household planning.
- It gives contract parties a neutral, trusted benchmark for price adjustments.
- It improves the accuracy of GDP and productivity figures.
- It shows how prices move between industries, which helps in analyzing tariffs, energy shocks and supply disruptions.

---

## 9. Access and formats (for data librarians and preservationists)

- **Portal:** bls.gov/ppi, including news releases, the Detailed Report (PDF and XLSX), the Handbook of Methods, and notices.
- **Flat files:** download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ — "pc/" for industry data and "wp/" for commodity and FD‑ID data. Discontinued series are kept in separate databases (see bls.gov/data/archived.htm).
- **API:** BLS Public Data API v2. Free registration raises the query and series limits.
- **Interactive tools:** Data Finder, Series Report, Top Picks.
- **Licensing:** U.S. government work, public domain. Citation is requested.
- **Historical archives:**
  - St. Louis Fed FRASER holds digitized WPI and PPI publications, Detailed Reports and shutdown notices.
  - Release archives are at bls.gov/bls/news-release/ppi.htm (for example, ppi_MMDDYYYY.htm).
- **Preservation priorities:**
  1. Discontinued series, since BLS said it would move them to archives only as resources allow.
  2. Index additions, deletions and recodes, published in Detailed Report Tables 18–20.
  3. Archived technical notes and handbook versions, which record changes in sample size, weights and methods.
  4. Monthly snapshots of first-release values. These are overwritten by revisions and seasonal factor updates.

# PPI Risk Assessment (as of early October 2026)

PPI is a core federal inflation measure, and the headline index is very unlikely to disappear. The detail behind it has already been cut, though, and the agency's staff, leadership and politics remain under strain. Four categories are rated Moderate or High.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for higher risk**
- BLS stopped publishing about 350 indexes between August 2025 and February 2026. These included final-demand "core" variants, textile series, industry indexes, and the whole hides, skins and leather group (04). BLS said it would move them to its archive of discontinued series "only… as resources allow."
- There was never a standalone October 2025 news release. The October 2025 Detailed Report is listed as "Not Available." The October numbers came out later, inside the November release on January 14, 2026.
- Each January, revisions to seasonal adjustment overwrite the previously published figures. This is normal practice, but it means first-release values survive only in archived copies.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- The main series are still online in BLS's flat files, API and data tools. The All Commodities index goes back to 1913.
- BLS keeps separate databases for discontinued series, including commodity series back through the SIC era. Its FAQ (updated March 2026) says history for deleted indexes "still will be available in the discontinued databases."
- I found no reports of historical files being taken down.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** No historical files are known to be gone. But hundreds of series ended, and whether all of their history has actually been moved to the archive depends on resources. I did not check whether it has been.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for higher risk**
- The 2025 government shutdown delayed the September 2025 release from October 16 to November 25, and wiped out the standalone October release.
- January 2026 data was originally set for February 12, 2026. The calendar now shows it released on February 27, 2026. I could not confirm why it moved.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- Since then, releases have run monthly on schedule. The August 2026 data came out September 10. Upcoming releases are set for October 15, November 13 and December 15, 2026.
- The survey's paperwork approval (OMB 1220-0008) was renewed on June 9, 2024. I estimate it runs to mid-2027, based on the usual three-year term, but I did not see the official expiration notice. No new renewal notice has appeared in the Federal Register yet; one should appear around late 2026 or early 2027.
- No release has been missing for more than a year, and the approval is not expired.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** Releases have been missed and delayed within the last year, but the approval is active and the monthly schedule has returned to normal.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for higher risk**
- About 350 indexes are permanently gone, which is a direct cut in detail.
- Collection has shrunk. The 2026 technical note cites "more than 44,000" price quotes a month, while the older Handbook text says about 50,000 items are priced monthly. These may count slightly different things, so the comparison is approximate.
- The American Statistical Association and the Labor Department's Inspector General (who opened a review in September 2025) both cite reduced CPI and PPI data collection.
- BLS's own planning says it will focus on core series and statutory needs, which leaves the remaining detail exposed to further cuts.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- Monthly frequency and the 8:30 a.m. release practice continue.
- In 2026 BLS updated the weights behind the final-demand structure and revised its release tables.

**Rating: High Risk.** Detail has been cut, and the rubric treats any cut in granularity as High Risk.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for higher risk**
- The legal authority is broad. The survey filing cites only 29 U.S.C. §2, the general duty to collect labor statistics, and no law names the PPI specifically.
- The survey is voluntary for businesses.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- PPI is designated a Principal Federal Economic Indicator, and BLS's FY2026–27 budget documents name these indicators as protected priorities.
- Federal programs depend on it:
  - BEA uses it to adjust GDP and other national accounts for inflation.
  - Price-adjustment clauses in federal contracts rely on it.
  - IRS rules for an inventory accounting method (LIFO, Treas. Reg. §1.472-8) are built on it.
  - CMS uses it in the cost indexes behind Medicare payment updates.
- Nothing else measures U.S. business-to-business prices at this level of detail.

**Rating: No Known Issue** for the headline and core indexes. Detailed indexes face something closer to **Moderate** risk: the cut series were evidently treated as expendable, and anyone whose contract or accounting method depends on one can lose it.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for higher risk**
- The Commissioner, Erika McEntarfer, was fired on August 1, 2025, after the President alleged, without evidence, that jobs data were rigged. This alone meets the "leadership removed" test for High.
- BLS has lost about 25% of its staff since February 2025, and nearly 40% of leadership posts are vacant (Friends of BLS, March 2026). Bloomberg Law reports 13 of 35 leadership roles vacant.
- Full-time staffing fell from 2,019 (FY2025) to 1,773 (FY2026), a drop of 246, or 12%. The FY2027 request is 1,754.
- The FY2026 request asked for an 8% cut, to $648M. The FY2027 request asks for $668M, 5.7% below FY2026, and would make the staff losses permanent.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- Congress actually gave BLS slightly more for FY2026 ($708.5M, up from $704M).
- A career BLS economist, Brett Matsumoto, was confirmed as Commissioner on August 7, 2026.

**Rating: High Risk.** The leadership was removed and roughly a quarter of staff are gone. I could not get BLS-specific figures from the staffing tracker you suggested: it stopped updating on December 31, 2025, and its data loads dynamically. These numbers come from the budget documents and advocacy group reports.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for higher risk**
- About 350 indexes were cut after January 2025, directly changing what is published. BLS cited resource limits, which followed the government-wide hiring freeze and buyouts.
- The removal of the Commissioner and public claims of rigged data have hurt trust in the agency.
- The administration's budgets for FY2026 and FY2027 propose moving BLS into the Commerce Department alongside Census and BEA, and limiting work to core indicators and statutory needs.

**Evidence for lower risk**
- No presidential action has targeted the PPI survey itself.
- The discontinuation notice gives resource reasons, not policy objections.
- Congress has not enacted the reorganization, and the new Commissioner is a career statistician.

**Rating: High Risk** (a borderline call). The rubric covers significant changes made in line with administration priorities, and the index cuts and leadership removal fit that. The Commerce proposal on its own would only be Moderate.

## Summary
- Historical Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
- Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
- Data Quality: **High Risk**
- Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**
- Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**
- Policy: **High Risk**
